title: flexible chaos: globalization and race in los angeles disaster film and fiction
display_name: Flexible Chaos: Globalization and Race in Los Angeles Disaster Film and Fiction
abstract: click to increase image sizeclick to decrease image size notes according to scott bukatman, the film's initial setting, the new york street set of burbank studios, was deliberately retrofitted as los angeles in order to more persuasively convey the feeling of a futuristic film noir slum (21). blade runner's visual emphasis of a decayed future was rendered more persuasive by its relocation to la, a majority minority city. the film's cinematic vision was acknowledged by multiple academy award nominations for art direction, set decoration, and visual effects. newsweek referred to sony's widely publicized acquisition of columbia pictures in 1989 as a japanese invasion of hollywood. see ellis cose's yellow-peril journalism. in many ways, the film's entire premise is a futuristic interpretation of the racial passing trope distinct to the african american literary tradition. only now, it is androids, constructed by humans for slave labor in their planetary colonies, who revolt and attempt to pass for the human race to achieve their freedom. for a discussion of the film in the context of racial passing and cyborgs, see leilani nishime's the mulatto cyborg. the film's engagement with the limits of humanity triggered by cybergenetics and postmodern capitalism has not ceased to fascinate cultural critics. see, for example, kaja silverman's back to the future, slavoj zizek's the thing that thinks, and david harvey's time and space in postmodern cinema. this image stands in stark contrast to the asian american shop owner in spike lee's seminal film, do the right thing (1989). armed with only his broom, he succeeds in deterring potential looters by shouting to them, i black! i black! during the riots, however, the media portrayed shop owners as defiantly and militantly asian, often armed with guns. song suggests that, for such reasons, the los angeles uprising served as a watershed historical moment of pessimism concerning the future on the part of asian american cultural producers. drawing from sandra govan, rutledge observes that the lack of people of color in speculative fiction set in the future is due to the fact that racism [is] considered not to be a problem of the future (238). in order to show how much a certain society has advanced, it often represents the eradication of racism by eradicating racialized bodies altogether. though critic richard schickel nods his head to the film's social satire, he argues that such political astuteness is undermined by the fact that virtually all the psychopathically murderous criminals [in the film are] minority-group members (98). police presence is a prominent trope in la disaster films. (in blade runner, deckard is a private blade runner contracted by the lapd.) because of its proximity to the military-industrial complex surrounding the city, as well as the region's role in u.s. imperialist endeavors throughout the pacific islands and asia, the lapd has led the nation, if not the world, in technological developments of organized police surveillance and discipline. the lapd was the first force in the nation to use police helicopters, in a response to the watts rebellion in 1965. due to the city's spatially dispersed form, the lapd was also the first to substitute mounted and foot patrol with patrol cars. such technological developments radically reshaped the role, scope, and significance of police interference in the city, in particular in its numerous ethnic neighborhoods. see mike davis's city of quartz. for a discussion of how the absence of asian americans, particularly japanese americans, was integral to the project of u.s. nation-building after wwii, see simpson's an absent presence. see also mae m. ngai's impossible subjects. for a discussion of the novel within the context of environmental justice (environmental racism), see julie sze's not by politics alone. transnationalism is the dominant theme of criticism on the novel. drawing upon border theory, claudia sadowski-smith argues that yamashita deploys mesoamerican myths in order to create a new mode of cross-cultural and transnational mythmaking that respond[s] to recent transformations in the u.s.-mexico borderlands (92). for literary criticism, caroline rody notes that the novel exemplifies the combined impact of the new transnational and interethnic paradigms on works of asian american literature and points towards more global and more visionary narrative possibilities (132, 139). in a more allegorical reading, florence hsiao-ching li emphasizes the trope of motherhood in the novel as a type of transnational border-crossing, a way to transgress the borders between the self and the other (164). sue-im lee locates what she refers to as a romantic universalism in the novel that can express the transnational, transcontinental nature of human existence without [the] imperialist dimensions indicative of earlier attempts at universalism (505, 503). within the context of globalization, molly wallace reads the novel as an example of the continental shift of north american cultural production due to nafta in particular and transnational capitalism in general (158). in her approach from critical race studies, ruth hsu argues that the book decenter[s] the dominant anglo euro-american narratives about los angeles, the ones that empower and maintain the dominant image of white and western superiority (77). my own reading most closely aligns with those of rody and wallace, but with an emphasis on the historical relationship between globalization and race. it is significant that the redrawing of the national border is due to the movement of citrus. a spanish colonial import to the americas, the orange historically served as a symbol of conquest, making pre-columbian another word for orangeless (rauch 28). yet supposedly, spanish oranges originally came from india, and indian oranges can be traced back to china. as molly rauch observes, the orange is an immigrant, through and through (28). the homage to performance artist guillermo g mez-pe a is clear, and a passage from his book, the new world border, serves as the novel's epigraph. yamashita has explicitly stated in interviews that arcangel was inspired by g mez-pe a. see jean vengua gier and carla alicia tejeda's an interview with karen tei yamashita. for a history of the workings of race in the consolidation of a white, working class, u.s. identity, see david roediger's the wages of whiteness. for a discussion of the novel focused on rafaela's journey north, see claudia sadowski-smith's the u.s.-mexico borderlands write back. as political scientist wendy brown articulates, there are those who are said to be ruled by culture and those who are said to rule themselves but enjoy culture (20). in other words, there exist those who have culture and those who are a culture (brown 151, emphasis in the original). additional informationnotes on contributorshee-jung serenity joohee-jung serenity joo is assistant professor of english at the university of manitoba in winnipeg, canada. her research and teaching interests include speculative fiction, globalization studies, and critical race studies.

title: in support of a wide notion of media accessibility: access to content and access to creation
display_name: In support of a wide notion of media accessibility: Access to content and access to creation
abstract: the prevailing narrow consideration of media accessibility (ma) as concerning only persons with sensory disabilities poses a series of epistemological and terminological issues, and limits the potential of ma to instigate social change. this article supports a wider view of ma that encompasses both people with and without disabilities who need access to audiovisual content. to articulate this wide notion of ma, a distinction is made between access to content and access to creation (dangerfield, 2017), and examples are drawn from two emerging disciplines: interlingual respeaking and accessible filmmaking (afm). as far as access to content is concerned, interlingual respeaking can contribute to making ma more visible, forcing hearing audiences to share the same need for access as audiences with hearing loss. as for afm, by proposing the integration of translation and accessibility as part of the filmmaking process, it provides a platform for deaf, blind and foreign audiences, as well as other groups, to join forces and increase their visibility within the film industry. however, a wide notion of ma must also include access to creation, that is, access to equipment, funding and job opportunities that can enable persons with sensory disabilities to create audiovisual products which, it is argued, can provide a more inclusive and empathetic audiovisual experience than the current model of ma.

title: public service media in a digital media environment: performance from an audience perspective
display_name: Public Service Media in a Digital Media Environment: Performance from an Audience Perspective
abstract: for decades, public service broadcasting has played an important role in the provision of news and information in many european countries. today, however, public service media (psm) are confronted with numerous challenges, including the need to legitimise their role in an increasingly digital media environment. against this background, this study examines the audience perspective on the topic with an international comparative approach. it analyses the population s assessment of, and attitudes towards, the performance of psm. the aim is to identify what relevance is attributed to psm by the public in the digital age and how they see psm s role in comparison to other more recent (digital) media offerings. an online survey was conducted in three specifically selected countries: germany, france, and the uk. overall, the findings show that respondents attribute a clear role to psm and distinguish it from other media offerings in the increasingly digital media environment. they rate the information quality offered by psm as higher than that of most other media offerings. respondents are more likely to value social media platforms for entertainment purposes than psm. the findings also reveal differences in the evaluation of psm depending on psm news use, interest in news, political interest, as well as on demographic variables. on the other hand, differences between the individual countries overall were surprisingly small, pointing to the fact that psm across the countries sampled are with deviations perceived to be performing better than (most) other media, despite being confronted with changes and challenges in their environment.
